title: Trump's EPA Repeals Greenhouse Gas Limits on Power Plants
summary:
The Trump administration is repealing limits on greenhouse gas emissions emitted by the nation's fossil fuel-fired power plants. The head of the Environmental Protection Agency called it the largest deregulatory action of the U.S. power sector in history. This action eliminates rules the EPA finalized during the Biden administration that required existing coal and new natural gas-fired power plants to significantly reduce their carbon dioxide pollution, starting in the 2030s.

Carbon dioxide from human activity is the main driver of global warming. Power plants are the second-largest source of planet-heating carbon dioxide emissions in the U.S., behind transportation. At a press conference on Monday, EPA Administrator Lee Zeldin said that actions to curtail planet-heating pollution under the Biden and Obama administrations led to higher energy prices and prevented the country from reaching its full energy potential. "The days of Biden and Obama working to destroy natural gas and coal are over," Zeldin said.

Zeldin made his remarks in Houston, where the U.S. is hosting the G20 Energy Summit. He said the EPA was also proposing to rescind all remaining greenhouse gas emissions standards for power plants. "All of them," he said.

Environmental groups say the move will increase pollutants that harm human health. "These rules are really important, not just for our climate, but also to protect public health from the dangers of local air pollution," says Gudrun Thompson, senior attorney at the Southern Environmental Law Center. They plan to challenge the decision in court.

The legal basis for limiting climate pollution from power plants started with the Supreme Court's 2007 Massachusetts v. EPA decision, which concluded the EPA is required to regulate carbon dioxide under the Clean Air Act. That led to the EPA's 2009 endangerment finding that designated greenhouse gas pollution as a threat to human health. In 2014, the Obama administration proposed the Clean Power Plan to cut carbon dioxide emissions from power plants by 32% from 2005 levels by 2030. That plan faced legal challenges and never went into effect, but the country met that goal well before 2030 as coal plants were replaced by natural gas and renewable energy.

Last month was the hottest ever recorded globally because of human-caused climate change and a developing El Niño pattern. Michael Gerrard, a law professor at Columbia University, said, "2026 is shaping up to be the warmest year in recorded history, and we ain't seen nothing yet."
why_it_matters: If the repeal survives legal challenges, the U.S. — one of the world's biggest emitters — could produce more planet-heating pollution just as climate records keep falling, while other countries watch whether American climate policy stays stable. The fight also tests how far a president can rewrite environmental rules without Congress, a question that will shape energy prices, jobs and the climate today's teenagers will inherit.

background_read: The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is the federal agency that protects U.S. air, water and land, and its administrator — Lee Zeldin, who runs the agency under President Donald Trump — sets its direction.

The Clean Air Act is the landmark federal law from the early 1970s that lets the EPA limit pollution. In Massachusetts v. EPA, a 2007 Supreme Court case, the court ruled that carbon dioxide counts as a pollutant under that law, which led the EPA to issue its 2009 'endangerment finding' declaring greenhouse gases a threat to public health.

Since then, power plant rules have swung back and forth with each administration. The Obama-era Clean Power Plan was put on hold by the Supreme Court before it ever took effect, and a later Supreme Court ruling (West Virginia v. EPA) said the EPA needed clear permission from Congress before it could force a nationwide shift away from coal.

The U.S. has also joined and left the Paris climate agreement — a global deal in which countries promise to cut emissions — more than once, showing how quickly climate policy can flip when the White House changes hands.

Scientists say carbon dioxide released by burning coal, oil and gas traps heat in the atmosphere, and that human activity is the main cause of the warming that keeps breaking global temperature records.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — the administration and fossil-fuel industry
perspectives.description: Zeldin argues the Biden and Obama rules raised energy prices and stopped the country from reaching its full energy potential, and he says the repeal lets natural gas and coal compete freely. Supporters claim emissions can keep falling through cheaper natural gas and new technology rather than through government mandates.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — environmental and public health groups
perspectives.description: Groups such as the Southern Environmental Law Center say the repeal will increase pollutants that harm human health, not just greenhouse gases, and they plan to challenge it in court. They point out that the EPA's own endangerment finding still declares greenhouse gases a threat to health and the climate.

The rules have moved back and forth for years: courts have both required the EPA to regulate carbon dioxide and limited how broadly it can act, with West Virginia v. EPA saying big economy-wide changes need clear permission from Congress. That means each administration re-fights the same battle, and judges, not voters, often settle it.

If the repeal holds, U.S. power plant emissions could rise just as global temperatures keep setting records. If courts strike it down, the EPA would have to write new rules again, and Congress could end the cycle by passing a law — which is why this fight is likely to continue long after Monday's announcement.
